q1: SELECT b1.name AS bar1, b2.name AS bar2 FROM bar AS b1, bar AS b2 WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT s1.beer FROM serves AS s1 WHERE s1.bar = b1.name AND NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM serves AS s2 WHERE s2.bar = b2.name AND s2.beer = s1.beer)) AND EXISTS(SELECT s2.beer FROM serves AS s2 WHERE s2.bar = b2.name AND NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM serves AS s1 WHERE s1.bar = b1.name AND s1.beer = s2.beer))
q2: SELECT s1.bar AS bar1, s2.bar AS bar2 FROM serves AS s1 JOIN serves AS s2 ON s1.beer = s2.beer AND s1.bar <> s2.bar GROUP BY s1.bar, s2.bar HAVING COUNT(s1.beer) < (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM serves WHERE bar = s2.bar)

explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent because they are checking for different conditions related to the beers served by bars. Q1 checks for bars that serve beers which no other bar serves, and Q2 checks for pairs of bars that serve the same beer but in different quantities.
counterexample_dsp: The test data should have at least two bars, 'Bar A' and 'Bar B', and a beer 'Beer X' that 'Bar A' serves but 'Bar B' does not serve. 'Bar A' should serve 'Beer X' in a quantity of 1, and 'Bar B' should serve 'Beer X' in a quantity of 2. This setup will trigger the difference between Q1 and Q2.
